title.en: The Monkey, the Turtle, and the Crocodile

region.en: Batangas town, Luzon, Philippines (where the story is common)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁鎮（故事流行之地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 58 'The Monkey, the Turtle, and the Crocodile', eBook #8299

summary.en: The deceiving monkey offers two exhausted travelers — a turtle and a crocodile — lodging and food, leading them to a field of ripe pumpkins, then goes home to sleep. The plantation owner arrives, summons laborers with long poles and bolos, and the two beasts flee clinging together — the turtle refusing to release the crocodile's tail, 'or else there will be no one to push you' — until the men overtake and kill them both.
summary.zh: 慣於欺騙的猴子假意款待兩位疲憊旅人——龜與鱷——領他們到熟南瓜田飽餐一頓後自回家睡覺。園主回來，召來持長棍與波洛刀的工人；二獸倉皇奔逃，龜仍死抓鱷尾——『不放，不然誰來推你』——終被追上，雙雙喪命。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator; archival record. A compensation story in which the monkey gets even with his two traditional opponents.

passages.text: There was once a monkey who used to deceive everybody whom he met, and as is the case with most deceivers, he had many enemies who tried to kill him. One day, walking in the streets of his native town, he met in a by-lane a turtle and a crocodile so tired they could hardly breathe. 'I'll try to deceive these slow creatures of the earth,' said the monkey to himself, and approached them with kind words. The two travelers, so much affected, told him all about themselves with the greatest candor: they were strangers from their native town, not knowing where to get food or spend the cold night. 'I'll conduct you to a place where you can spend the night and get all you want to eat,' said the monkey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 58 'The Monkey, the Turtle, and the Crocodile'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He brought them to a field full of ripe pumpkins — 'Eat all the pumpkins you want, and then rest here. Meanwhile I'll go home and take my sleep, too' — and while the two hungry travelers enjoyed a hearty meal, the owner of the plantation happened to pass by. Seeing the crocodile, he called to his laborers to bring long poles and their bolos. The turtle clung to the tail of the crocodile, and away they went. 'Don't cling to my tail! I cannot run fast if you cling to my tail. Let go! for the men will soon overtake us,' said the crocodile. 'I have to cling to your tail, or else there will be no one to push you,' said the turtle. But their attempt to escape was unsuccessful: the men overtook them and killed them both. Such was the unhappy end of the turtle and the crocodile. Moral: Never trust a new friend or an old enemy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 58 'The Monkey, the Turtle, and the Crocodile'; not verbatim.

region.en: Binalonan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (where the story is fairly common)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省比納隆安（故事流行之地）

texts.period: Pangasinan oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 59 'The Iguana and the Turtle', eBook #8299

summary.en: Caught poaching in a pond-owner's pond, the turtle persuades the wife-hungry iguana to swap places by pretending he is tied there for refusing to marry the old man's daughter. The iguana cries 'I want to marry your daughter' until beaten at; later the turtle tricks him into putting his mouth between two wind-rubbed bamboos to hear 'the pipe of my grandfather up there' — his mouth badly pinched, he falls, and the turtle disappears.
summary.zh: 海龜在塘主池中偷魚被捕，拴於屋下；他謊稱『老翁逼婚、我不肯』，誘得想娶妻的鬣蜥換位受縛。鬣蜥連喊『我要娶你的女兒』直至挨打掙脫；再遇海龜時，又被騙去聽風中相磨的雙竹——『那是我祖父的笛聲』——竹片夾嘴，跌落於地，海龜早已不見蹤影。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan fable recorded by Fansler from a Guico narrator; archival record. Fansler compares the related Tinguian tale (Fay-Cooper Cole, No. 78) and a Borneo mouse-deer story.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived two good friends, an iguana and a turtle, who always went fishing together. One day the turtle invited the iguana to catch fish in a certain pond that he knew of; after about two hours the old man who owned the pond came along, the iguana escaped, but the turtle was caught. The old man took the turtle home, tied a string around its neck, and fastened it under the house. Early in the morning the iguana wandered everywhere looking for his friend and finally found him under the old man's house, tied to a post.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 59 'The Iguana and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'What are you doing here, my friend?' said the iguana. 'That old man wants me to marry his daughter, but I do not want to marry her,' said the turtle. The iguana, who very much wanted a wife, was delighted at this chance, and asked to be allowed to take the turtle's place; the turtle consented, the iguana released the turtle and was tied up in his place, and the turtle made off as fast as he could. When the old man woke up he heard some one saying over and over again, 'I want to marry your daughter'; angry, he went down and found the iguana saying it, and picked up a big stick to beat its head — but the iguana cut the string and ran away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 59 'The Iguana and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On his way he came across the turtle again, listening to the sound produced by the rubbing of two bamboos when the wind blew. 'What! are you here again?' said the iguana. 'Be quiet! I am listening to the pipe of my grandfather up there. Don't you hear it?' said the turtle. The iguana wanted to see the turtle's grandfather, so he climbed up the tree and put his mouth between the two bamboos that were rubbing together; his mouth was badly pinched, and he fell down to the ground. The turtle meanwhile had disappeared. Moral: This teaches that the one who believes foolishly will be injured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 59 'The Iguana and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Trial among the Animals: Sinukuan's Court on Mt. Arayat
title.zh: 動物受審：阿拉亞特山蘇努庫安法庭

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特山

texts.period: Pampangan oral legend; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60a 'The Trial among the Animals', eBook #8299

summary.en: Sinukuan, driven from his town by envy of his strength, dwells in a cave of Mount Arayat, wins the friendship of the animals by taking whatever form they do, and is made their judge. A noisy frog blames the turtle carrying his house, the turtle blames the firefly playing with fire, the firefly blames the mosquito's dagger — each freed with a good reason — until the mosquito, without excuse, is sentenced to three days' imprisonment and loses his voice: since then the male mosquito has had none and fears to carry his dagger.
summary.zh: 蘇努庫安因力大遭人妒恨，退居阿拉亞特山洞穴，能化身任何前來的動物，被眾獸奉為法官。夜噪的蛙推諿於『背屋的龜』，龜推諿於『玩火的螢』，螢推諿於『帶匕首的蚊』——個個理由得直、當庭開釋；唯有蚊子無辭可辯，被判三日監禁，從此失聲——公蚊啞然，且不敢再帶匕首。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan tale recorded by Fansler from a Pineda narrator; archival record. Sinukuan is the great Pampangan mountain-spirit of Mt. Arayat; sacred-place tag marks the cave court. The 'clock' story chain has four further Philippine variants (The Pugu's Case, Why Mosquitoes Hum, A Tyrant, The Bacuit's Case).

passages.text: In ancient times Sinukuan, the judge of the animals, lived in one of the caves of Mount Arayat. He had formerly lived in a neighboring town; but, since he was so brave and strong, the people began to envy him, then to hate him, and at last made so many plots against his life that he gave up all his property and friends in the town, and went to live in Mount Arayat, where he devoted all his time to gaining the friendship of the animals there. It was not hard for Sinukuan to win the love of the animals, for he had the power of changing himself into whatever form he pleased, and always took the form of those animals who came to him; before long all the animals realized the power, wisdom, and justice of their good companion, and made him their judge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'The Trial among the Animals'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day a bird came to Sinukuan's court and asked him to punish the frog for being so noisy during the night. The frog answered respectfully, 'Sir, I was only crying for help, because the turtle was carrying his house on his back, and I feared that I might be buried under it' — and was freed. The turtle, in turn, replied that he carried his house because the firefly was playing with fire and he was afraid it might set fire to his home: 'Is it not right to protect one's house from fire?' — and was freed. The firefly said he had no other means to protect himself from the sharp-pointed dagger of the mosquito — and was liberated too. Finally the mosquito was tried; and, since he did not have any good reason to give for carrying his dagger, Sinukuan sentenced him to three days' imprisonment. The mosquito was obliged to submit; and it was during this confinement that he lost his voice. Ever since, the male mosquito has had no voice, and he has been afraid to carry his dagger, for fear of greater punishment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'The Trial among the Animals'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why Mosquitoes Hum and Try to Get into the Holes of Our Ears

region.zh: 菲律賓薄荷島（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Visayan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60c 'Why Mosquitoes hum and try to get into the Holes of our Ears', eBook #8299

summary.en: Crab-king Mangla of old Bohol orders the bataktak to guard his house in silence; their laughter at a snoring king during heavy rain leads to a trial-chain: the bataktak laughed seeing Hu-man carrying his house, Hu-man for fear of Aninipot's fire, Aninipot because Lamoc the mosquito kept biting him. When Lamoc is summoned he pre-arranges his companions to follow, bites the king's face, and is killed by the sheriff Cagang, whose pursuers cannot enter his deep burrow — they remain humming around the doors; the mosquitoes mistake the holes of our ears for the house of Cagang, and that is why they hum about our ears.
summary.zh: 古時薄荷島蟹王曼格拉令小蟹守夜禁聲；大雨之夜眾蟹見『人背屋』而笑，被審——人因怕螢火蟲背屋、螢火蟲因蚊叮而持火。蚊王拉莫克早令同伴跟隨，到場便咬王面，被郡守卡岡誅殺；其同伴追至卡岡深居的地下巢穴，無法攻入，遂終日繞門嗡嗡——今人耳孔被誤作卡岡之家，蚊聲因此繞耳不絕。

sensitivity.note: Visayan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Torralba narrator (Bohol); archival record. Explains mosquito humming as the siege of the crab-sheriff's burrow.

passages.text: In those very early times, in the province of Bohol, there lived a creature called Mangla; he was king of the crabs. One night, tired and sleepy, Mangla ordered his old sheriff Cagang, leader of the small land-crabs, to call his followers, the Bataktak, before him, and told them: 'You must all watch my house while I am sleeping; but do not make any noise that will waken me.' While he was snoring, it began to rain so hard that the guards could not help laughing. The king awoke very angry, but being still tired and sleepy, waited till morning, and then asked the Bataktak why they had laughed when he had told them not to make any noise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'Why Mosquitoes Hum'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Bataktak answered softly, 'We could not help laughing, because last night we saw our old friend Hu-man carrying his house on his shoulder' — and the king pardoned them, then summoned Hu-man, who replied humbly that he was carrying his house because Aninipot was bringing fire and he was afraid his only dwelling would be burned. Aninipot, summoned next, answered in a trembling voice that he was carrying fire because Lamoc was always trying to bite him, and to protect himself he would carry fire all the time. The king realized there was a great deal of trouble brewing in his kingdom, and sent for Lamoc — who, before leaving his own house, had told all his companions to follow him, for he expected trouble.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'Why Mosquitoes Hum'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before Lamoc reached the palace the king was already shouting with rage, so Lamoc approached the king and bit his face. Mangla cried out, 'It is true, what I heard from Bataktak, Hu-man, and Aninipot!' and ordered his sheriff to kill Lamoc; Cagang killed him, but Lamoc's companions, bent on avenging the murder, rushed at him and followed him to his home — very deep under the ground, where they could not get in, so they remained and hummed around the door. Even to-day at the doors of the houses of Cagang and his followers there are many friends of Lamoc humming and trying to go inside. It is said that the Lamoc mistake the holes of our ears for the house of Cagang, and that that is the reason mosquitoes hum about our ears now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'Why Mosquitoes Hum'; not verbatim.

title.en: A Tyrant: The King Who Died Swatting a Mosquito

region.en: Jaen, Nueva Ecija, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋新怡詩夏省哈恩（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60d 'A Tyrant', eBook #8299

summary.en: A tyrant's law of silence is extended to the animals; a croaking frog is tried, and excuses himself for laughing at the snail carrying his house; the snail fears the firefly's fire; the firefly fears the mosquito's bite. Tired of the trial, the king forbids the mosquito ever to bite again and seizes his mallet; the mosquito alights on the king's forehead, the blow kills the insect — and ends the tyranny with it.
summary.zh: 暴君禁聲之律竟施於動物。蛙因『笑蝸牛背屋』受審；蝸牛怕螢火燒屋；螢火怕蚊叮。國王厭倦長審，下令蚊蟲永不許叮人，並舉槌欲擊；蚊飛落國王額頭，一槌下去蚊死——暴政亦隨之而終。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale recorded by Fansler from an Esquivel narrator; archival record. Fourth link of the 'clock' story chain; moral: It is foolish to carry matters to extremes.

passages.text: Once there lived a tyrannical king. One of his laws prohibited the people from talking loudly; even when this law had been put in force he was still not satisfied, so he ordered the law to be enforced among the animals. One of his officers once heard a frog croak, caught it, and carried it before the king. 'Don't you know that there is a law prohibiting men and animals from making a noise?' began the trial. 'Yes, your Majesty, but I could not help laughing to see the snail carrying his house with him wherever he goes,' said the frog — and the king was satisfied and dismissed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'A Tyrant'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The snail said he was always afraid the firefly was going to burn his house; the firefly said the mosquitoes would bite him if he did not carry his fire; and the mosquito, asked why he was always trying to bite some one, said, 'Why, sir, I cannot live without biting somebody.' The king was tired of the long trial, so with the mosquito he determined to end it: 'From now on you must not bite anybody. You have no right to do so.' When the mosquito tried to protest the sentence, the king seized his mallet and determined to crush him with it; but the mosquito alighted on the forehead of the king. The king became very angry at this insult and hit the mosquito hard — he killed the mosquito, but he also put an end to his own tyranny. Moral: It is foolish to carry matters to extremes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 60 'A Tyrant'; not verbatim.

region.en: Taal, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省塔阿爾（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 61 'The Greedy Crow', eBook #8299

summary.en: A crow eating his meat sees a kasaykasay fly past with a dead rat; enraged at being ignored, he abandons his own meal to chase the faster little bird, fails, and returns to find a hawk has carried off the meat — and the hawk, passing again, taunts him: 'I am very sorry for you.'
summary.zh: 烏鴉正食腐肉，見小雀卡賽卡賽叼死鼠掠過；小雀不理會他的呼喝，烏鴉怒而棄食追趕，卻追不上。折返樹頭，肉已被路過的老鷹叼走；鷹再度經過時嘲笑道：『現在告訴你是我拿的——我真為你難過。』

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Gaa narrator; archival record. Fansler considers it native, distantly related to the Culladhanuggaha-jataka (No. 374) and 'The Dog and his Shadow.'

passages.text: One day a crow found a piece of meat on the ground, picked it up, and flew to the top of a tree to eat it. A kasaykasay, a small bird, passed by carrying a dead rat and flying very fast. The crow called to her, 'Kasaykasay, where did you get that dead rat that you have?' But the small bird did not answer: she flew on her way. When the crow saw that she paid no attention to him, he was very angry, and called out, 'Kasaykasay, Kasaykasay, stop and give me a piece of that rat, or I will follow you and take the whole thing for myself!' Still the small bird paid no attention to him. At last, full of greed and rage, the crow determined to have the rat by any means, and left the meat he was eating to fly after the small creature — but although she was only a little bird, the Kasaykasay could fly faster than the crow, and he could not catch her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 61 'The Greedy Crow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: While the crow was chasing the Kasaykasay, a hawk happened to pass by the tree where the crow had left his meat, saw it, and at once seized it in his claws and flew away. Though the crow pursued the Kasaykasay a long time, he could not overtake her, and gave up at last; but when he came to the spot and found the meat gone, he was almost ready to die of disappointment and hunger. By and by the hawk which had taken the meat passed the tree again and called to the crow, 'Mr. Crow, do you know that I am the one who took your meat? If not, I will tell you now, and I am very sorry for you.' The crow did not answer, for he was so tired and weak that he could hardly breathe. Moral: Do not be greedy. Be contented with what you have, and do not wish for what you do not own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 61 'The Greedy Crow'; not verbatim.

region.en: Cavite province, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋甲米地省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 62 'The Humming-Bird and the Carabao', eBook #8299

summary.en: A tiny humming-bird bets the carabao he can drink more river water. The carabao drinks against the rising tide until he nearly bursts — 'you have added more water to the river instead' — while the little bird merely dips his bill and waits for the ebb, 'drinking' as the river empties. The beaten carabao is left stupefied by all the water he swallowed.
summary.zh: 蜂鳥誇口喝水勝過水牛。漲潮之際，水牛拚命吞飲，肚子將裂——『你沒喝，倒往河裡添水了』——蜂鳥僅將喙點入水中，靜候退潮，『喝乾』了整條河。水牛被大量河水脹得頭昏眼花，認輸認得莫名其妙。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog fable recorded by Fansler from a Lopez narrator (Cavite); archival record. Fansler compares the nearly identical North Borneo tale 'The Kandowei and the Kerbau.'

passages.text: One hot April morning a carabao was resting under the shade of a quinine-tree which grew near the mouth of a large river, when a humming-bird alighted on one of the small branches above him. After the friendly greeting, little Hum said he was so thirsty that he had come down to drink, and the carabao answered jestingly, 'I wonder how much you can drink! You are so small, that a drop ought to be more than enough to satisfy you.' 'Yes, Friend Carabao? I bet you that I can drink more than you can! You drink first, and we shall see.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 62 'The Humming-Bird and the Carabao'; not verbatim.

passages.text: So old carabao, ignorant of the trick that was being played on him, walked to the bank of the river and began to drink. He drank and drank and drank; but it so happened that the tide was rising, and, no matter how much he swallowed, the water in the river kept getting higher and higher. At last he could drink no more, and the humming-bird began to tease him: 'Why, Friend Carabao, you have not drunk anything. It seems to me that you have added more water to the river instead.' 'You fool!' answered the carabao angrily, 'can't you see that my stomach is almost bursting?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 62 'The Humming-Bird and the Carabao'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the humming-bird only pretended to drink. He knew that the tide would soon be going out, so he just put his bill in the water, and waited until the tide did begin to ebb. The water of the river began to fall also. The carabao noticed the change, but he could not comprehend it; he was surprised, and agreed that he had been beaten. Little Hum flew away, leaving poor old Carabao stupefied and hardly able to move, because of the great quantity of water he had drunk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 62 'The Humming-Bird and the Carabao'; not verbatim.

region.en: Ilagan, Isabela, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋伊莎貝拉省伊拉甘（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Ilocano oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 63 'The Camanchile and the Passion', eBook #8299

summary.en: A flowerless camanchile-tree laments that travelers pass him by, and the low-growing Passion vine climbs him to display her blossoms on his crown. Months later the tree realizes he is being smothered and begs her to leave; Passion will not go, and Camanchile dies. Moral: Be yourself.
summary.zh: 無花的卡曼奇勒樹嘆息旅人不屑一顧；低矮的西番蓮藤攀上樹冠，以花朵為其添彩。數月後樹木窒息難耐，哀求藤蔓離開；西番蓮不肯，卡曼奇勒遂枯死。寓意：做你自己。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano fable recorded by Fansler from a Maramag narrator; archival record. Fansler compares the Palasa-jataka (No. 370) on a tree destroyed by a parasitic banyan-shoot.

passages.text: Once upon a time there grew in a forest a large camanchile-tree with spreading branches. Near it grew many other trees with beautiful fragrant flowers that attracted travellers; the camanchile had no fragrant flowers, but its crown was beautifully shaped, for the leaves received as much light as the leaves of the other trees. Yet the beauty of the crown proved of no attraction, and travellers passed the tree by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 63 'The Camanchile and the Passion'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Camanchile exclaimed aloud, 'Oh, what a dreary life I lead! I would that I had flowers like the others, so that travellers would visit me often!' A vine by the name of Passion, which grew near by and received only a small amount of light, heard the exclamation and thought this its opportunity to improve its condition: 'Oh, that's easy! Just let me climb on you, and I'll display on your crown my beautiful flowers. Then many persons will come to see you.' Camanchile consented, and after a few days Passion reached the top of the tree and soon covered the crown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 63 'The Camanchile and the Passion'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A few months later Camanchile realized that he was being smothered: he could not get light, so he asked Passion to leave him. 'O Passion! what pain I am in! I can't get light. Your beauty is of no value. I am being smothered: so leave me, I beg of you!' Passion would not leave Camanchile, however, and so Camanchile died. Moral: Be yourself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 63 'The Camanchile and the Passion'; not verbatim.

title.en: Auac and Lamiran: The Hawk Who Sang Away His Fish
title.zh: 奧瓦克與拉米蘭：唱掉魚的鷹

region.en: Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (where the story is well known)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特（故事著名之地）

texts.period: Pampangan oral fable; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 64 'Auac and Lamiran', eBook #8299

summary.en: The hawk Auac, dining on a stolen salted fish, is flattered by the squirrel Lamiran — his shiny feathers, his kingly gait — until he is asked to sing. Opening his beak with 'Uac-uac-uac-uac!', he drops the fish, and Lamiran gets it. A heron on a carabao's back delivers the moral: do not always believe what others tell you, and remember that ill-gotten gains never prosper.
summary.zh: 鷹奧瓦克享用偷來的鹹魚時，被松鼠拉米蘭連番奉承——羽毛油亮、步態如王——直至被請求一展歌喉。牠張口『哇—哇—哇』，魚落於地，為松鼠所得。近旁水牛背上的蒼鷺贈言：勿盡信他人之言，且記『不義之財終不昌』。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan fable recorded by Fansler from a Villegas narrator; archival record. Philippine form of the Fox-and-Crow type; Fansler compares the Jambu-khadaka-jataka (No. 294) and Anta-jataka (No. 295).

passages.text: Once Auac, a hawk, stole a salted fish which was hanging in the sun to dry, and flew with it to a branch of a camanchile-tree, where he sat down and began to eat. As he was eating, Lamiran, a squirrel who had his house in a hole at the foot of the tree, looked up and said, 'What beautiful shiny black feathers you have, Auac!' When he heard this praise the hawk looked very dignified, nevertheless he was much pleased, and fluttered his wings. 'You are especially beautiful, Auac, when you walk; for you are very graceful,' continued the squirrel, and Auac, not understanding the trick, hopped along the branch with the air of a king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 64 'Auac and Lamiran'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I heard some one say yesterday that your voice is so soft and sweet, that every one who listens to your song is charmed. Please let me hear some of your notes, you handsome Auac!' said the cunning Lamiran. Auac, feeling more proud and dignified than ever, opened his mouth and sang, 'Uac-uac-uac-uac!' As he uttered his notes, the fish in his beak fell to the ground, and Lamiran got it. A heron which was standing on the back of a water-buffalo near by saw the affair, and said, 'Auac, let me give you a piece of advice. Do not always believe what others tell you, but think for yourself; and remember that ill-gotten gains never prosper.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 64 'Auac and Lamiran'; not verbatim.
